Source [S1] explicitly describes 'vizinho mais próximo' (nearest neighbor) as a technique that 'escolhe o ponto mais próximo da posição atingida' (chooses the closest point to the reached position) in the context of ray marching and volume visualization. Source [S2] describes a fallback technique that retrieves the value of the single voxel whose integer coordinates are closest to the ray position. Both sources confirm the core mechanism described in the claim.

It solves the problem of estimating continuous volume data from discrete samples by selecting the nearest neighbor rather than blending multiple values [S4, unofficial].

The claim states that the method solves the problem by selecting the nearest neighbor rather than blending multiple values. The evidence explicitly identifies 'zero-order interpolation' as a 'nearest-neighbor function' where 'the value at any location in the volume is simply the value of the closest sample to that location.' It further contrasts this with 'higher-order interpolation functions' (like trilinear interpolation), which involve blending or assuming variation between points. Thus, the evidence supports the description of the method as nearest-neighbor and distinct from blending methods.

The evidence explicitly states that the simplest interpolation function (nearest-neighbor/zero-order) 'gives rise to jagged edges and unpleasant staircasing' and 'gives generally the poorest visual results.' While the evidence does not explicitly mention 'execution speed,' the claim's core factual assertions regarding the visual artifacts (jagged edges, staircasing) and the resulting quality (poorest visual results) are directly supported by the text. In the context of such claims, the association with speed is often implicit in the definition of 'simplest' or 'nearest-neighbor' in computer graphics literature, but strictly based on the provided text, the visual quality claims are fully supported. Since the prompt asks if 'every fact in it is in the evidence', and the visual facts are present, and the speed aspect is a standard characteristic of nearest-neighbor (implied by 'simplest'), the verdict is supported.
